title: Empath test: am I an empath? Free empathy quiz — cv.cm
description: Free empath test: rate 14 statements about picking up on other people's feelings to get a score from 0 to 56, what it means and how to protect your energy. No sign-up; answers stay in your browser.
h1: Empath test: am I an empath?
lede: Do you feel other people's moods as if they were your own, and leave a sad conversation drained? Rate 14 statements to see how strongly you tune in to others, and how to look after yourself if the answer is very.
about: "Empath" is a popular word, not a scientific category, for someone who takes in other people's emotions very strongly. Psychologists study the same ground as empathy, which they usually split into two parts: affective empathy, feeling what someone else feels, and cognitive empathy, understanding what they feel and why. People differ a lot on both, and very high affective empathy can be tiring if you don't also have ways to step back.

The statements here were written for cv.cm around everyday signs of strong empathy. They are not taken from any published empathy scale, and half of them describe low empathy so that simply agreeing with everything lands in the middle. The score bands are a rough guide, not research cut-offs. Being an empath is not a diagnosis, and it is not a superpower either: it is one end of an ordinary human trait.

faq.a: Someone who senses and takes on other people's emotions very strongly, often before anyone says a word. The term comes from popular psychology; researchers would describe it as very high affective empathy.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4, and half are reversed, so the total runs from 0 to 56. 18 or less is low, 19 to 37 is in the middle, and 38 or more is high.

faq.q: Is an empath the same as a highly sensitive person?
faq.a: They overlap, but they are not the same. High sensitivity is about how deeply you process everything around you, including noise, light and detail; being an empath is about other people's feelings in particular. You can try the highly sensitive person test on this site too.

faq.q: How can empaths protect their energy?
faq.a: Notice which feelings are yours and which you picked up, take short breaks after heavy conversations, and remember that caring for someone doesn't mean carrying their feelings for them. Time alone, sleep and saying no to some requests all help.

items: I often pick up on how someone feels before they say a word.
Other people's moods rarely rub off on me.
When a friend is upset, I feel their pain almost as if it were my own.
I find it easy to stay detached when someone tells me their problems.
People I have only just met often open up to me about personal things.
Hearing about strangers' hardships doesn't affect me much.
I can sense tension in a room as soon as I walk in.
I usually need people to tell me directly how they feel.
After comforting someone, I sometimes feel drained for hours.
I rarely find myself carrying other people's worries.
I find it hard to watch someone being embarrassed, even on TV.
I'm not usually the one friends come to when they need to talk.
I often know what someone needs before they ask.
I find it hard to imagine how a situation feels from someone else's side.

low.name: Grounded (0–18)
low.body: Other people's feelings don't easily knock you off balance. That keeps you steady in a crisis and makes you a calm person to lean on. If people sometimes say you seem distant, try asking how they feel and reflecting it back before offering solutions.

mid.name: Empathetic (19–37)
mid.body: You tune in to other people well but can still step back when you need to. That balance is a real strength: you can care about someone without being swept away by their mood. Keep noticing when a conversation leaves you heavy, and give yourself time to reset.

high.name: Likely empath (38–56)
high.body: You take in other people's emotions deeply and often before they speak. That makes you warm, perceptive and easy to confide in, and it can also leave you drained. Set gentle limits, take breaks after hard conversations and check whether a feeling is yours or one you picked up. If you feel overwhelmed most of the time, a counselor can help.
